newsitem.title: HUNGARY: Adviser in Hungary APV scandal shuns hearing.
newsitem.headline: Adviser in Hungary APV scandal shuns hearing.

text.p: The adviser at the centre of a scandal within Hungary's state privatisation agency APV over illegal payments on Wednesday failed to appear before a parliamentary committee investigating the affair
Marta Tocsik had been called to appear before the Constitutional and Justice Committee but cited reasons of health and her "psychological state" for not attending.

In January Tocsik was commissioned by APV without competitive bidding to negotiate with the local councils with a view to reducing the amount of assets to be transferred to local councils following privatisation.
Under a law passed in 1989, local councils must be recompensed for the land where formerly state-owned companies are located.
As a result of her work Tocsik received a "success fee" of 804 million forints ($5.2 million), or 10 percent of the money she saved.
Chairman of APV's executive board Imre Szokai and APV general manager Istvan Kocsis both appeared before the committee but Szokai declined to answer questions as he is under criminal investigation.
Hungary's Chief Prosecutor said on Tuesday he had ordered an investigation of the activities of Tocsik and other unnamed APV officials.
Kocsis told the committee that the 10 percent success fee in Tocsik's negotiations with local authorities on the transfer of assets was unusual.
"In normal privatisation contracts with advisers a success fee is two to three percent," he said, adding, however, that this was not a typical contract.
"This was an asset transfer and in this case APV did not have experience," he said.

Kocsis also told the committee that before being appointed as an adviser on asset transfers to local authorities, Tocsik had applied to act as a consultant in the privatisation of the energy sector late in 1995.
He said APV's legal department referred Tocsik to him as a potential adviser in the registration process of special state shares in the energy companies but there was no contract signed with her.
"Tocsik did not take part in the preparations of the energy sell-offs in any form," Kocsis told Reuters before the hearing.
The deals saw Western utilities buy into Hungary's gas and electricity industry to the tune of more than $2 billion and put Hungary at the forefront of post-communist large scale privatisation.
